opening.headline: We explore, from a prefix perspective, why significant savings are not observed even with prompt caching enabled, and we examine prompt structures that improve hit rates.
body: Public context-intensive services resend thousands of tokens of instructions and reference materials with every request. Re-processing the same input repeatedly results in recurring costs and delays. Prompt caching reduces this repetition, but its effectiveness is not guaranteed simply by enabling it. Some services perform well, while others show little improvement.

In this class, we first examine what cache stores and when it is reused. Then, we explore prompt structures that improve cache hit rates and methods for measuring cache hit rates, based on documentation from Google, OpenAI, and Anthropic. We also discuss cases where hit rates are low due to different system prompts across services.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain caching strategies used in large-scale services
There is a distinction between prompt structures that increase hit rates and those that decrease hit rates.

screens.title: The shared context is large but has low cache efficiency.
screens.lead: First, take a look at the situation of a service that shows no effect even with caching enabled. The diagram compares the request structures of three services side by side.

visual.alt: These three services use the same policy document, but due to differing content at the beginning of each request, the common parts are scattered at the end.
labels: The content is the same, but due to a preceding different cell, it is not reusable.

paragraphs: The company's customer support, sales, and HR services all respond by reading the same company policy document. The document is several thousand tokens long, so sending it with every request would significantly increase input costs. The team assumed that costs would have decreased because prompt caching is enabled by default.
Upon reviewing the invoice, I noticed almost no reduction. One service had a slight match, while the rest showed almost no match. Why wasn't the document reused in this case?

Caching does not occur when the entire request is similar. There must be a contiguous sequence starting from the beginning of the prompt with no character differences. Even if the common document that follows is identical, caching will not occur if each service starts its system prompt with a different sentence.

callout.label: Questions to be answered in this class
callout.text: What prompt structure increases accuracy, and how should it be designed to be used across multiple services?

screens.outro: First, let's recall what our current service is like.

screens.title: Think back to whether cache hit ratio is being measured.
screens.lead: First, think through each question on your own before selecting an answer. The instructor's thoughts will then be organized and presented. No answers are submitted.

items.prompt: Are you measuring cache hit rate numerically?
items.answer: You cannot know whether caching is enabled and whether it has an effect without measuring it. Since hit ratio is direct evidence of cost savings, viewing the numbers should be the starting point.

items.prompt: Do you know that you can verify the number of tokens processed from cache in the response?
items.answer: All three providers respond or handle token information in the cache via a dashboard. Gemini stores values in fields such as `usage.total_cached_tokens`, while Anthropic stores values in fields such as `cache_read_input_tokens`. Whether these fields are logged in service logs is the first item to be checked.

items.prompt: Have you compared how system prompts differ across services?
items.answer: When creating separate services, it's easy for the prompt's initial portions to differ across services. By overlapping and comparing the first 1,000 tokens shared among services, you can immediately see how much content is reusable.

items.prompt: Are requests with the same prefix being repeated within a short period of time?
items.answer: Cache entries do not persist for long. Even if they share the same prefix, they must be reprocessed if the request interval exceeds their lifespan. It is necessary to verify whether the call interval matches the cache lifetime.

screens.outro: To answer this question, we first need to understand what cache stores.

screens.title: Prompt caching reuses prefixes.
screens.lead: The following flashcards explain the core concepts and provider-specific approaches to prompt caching. Select a card to flip it over. Use the right arrow to advance to the next card.

cards.back: This is the unchanging prefix that follows continuously from the beginning of the prompt. Caching only reuses this prefix when the prefix is identical; if only one character in the prefix differs, the remainder is considered mismatched.

Stores the intermediate state (KV state) of the generated model during input processing. It does not store the response or tokens themselves. If the next request shares the same prefix, it reuses the stored state and only processes the newly arrived portion.

Enabled by default in the support model. Reused tokens are subject to reduced cache input costs, with up to 95% discount. Cache prefixes must meet a minimum length requirement, and models after GPT-5.6 require a length of 1,024 tokens. Monitor hit rates via the dashboard and use the diagnostic tool to identify mishit causes.

Implicit caching is enabled by default for all models released after Gemini 2.5. No configuration is required—reductions are automatically delivered upon successful matching. Each model has a minimum input token count, which is specified in the documentation as either 4,096 or 2,048.

If you add the `cache_control` field at the top level of the request, a breakpoint is automatically applied to the last cachable block. You can also explicitly specify a breakpoint on individual blocks using `cache_control`. The default lifespan is 5 minutes, and selecting a 1-hour lifespan results in twice the default input price.

screens.outro: If prefixes are key, let us now examine how to construct prompts to improve accuracy.

screens.title: Prompt structures that improve accuracy rate
screens.lead: The following two prompts are examples of the same content arranged in a different order. First, read the poor structure where the prefix changes each time, and select the emphasized section to verify the reason.

visual.alt: A diagram comparing vertically the situation where, in a bad structure, all the trailing values are reprocessed due to the frontmost variable change, and in a good structure, the front common portion is reused.

data.text:
Bad structure
[System] Current time: 2026-10-22 09:14:03, Request ID: req-48213
[System] Service: Customer Support, Tone: Friendly
[Common Policy Document] Refund Policy, Security Policy, Vacation Policy Documents
[Common Rules] Responses must be in Korean, and the relevant clause must be stated together
[User Question] What is the deadline for refund requests?

Good structure
[Common Policy Document] Refund Rules, Security Rules, Vacation Rules  
[General Rules] Responses must be in Korean, with relevant clause references provided  
[Service-Specific Guidelines] Service: Customer Support, Tone: Friendly
[Value by request] Current time: 2026-10-22 09:14:03, Request ID: req-48213
[User Question] What is the deadline for refund requests?

marks.note: The current timestamp and request ID at the front vary with each request. Since the prefix changes from the beginning, even if the subsequent common documents and rules are identical, they are not reusable.
Placing service-specific guidelines before general content means each service will have a different prefix, making it impossible to share caches between them.

marks.span:
[Common Policy Document] Refund Rules, Security Rules, Vacation Rules  
[General Rules] Responses must be in Korean, with relevant clause references provided  
[Service-Specific Guidelines]
marks.note: In a good design, we grouped large and common content at the front. Since this section is the same across all services, once processed, it can be reused by everyone.

marks.span: [Value by request] Current time: 2026-10-22 09:14:03, Request ID: req-48213
marks.note: Values that vary per request are sent backward. If the changing value is outside the prefix, reuse of the front common portion is not prevented.

screens.outro: The structure follows three rules: common content comes first, variable content comes after, and similar prefixes must be sent within the cache lifetime. Now let's see how hit rate is measured.

screens.title: Hit rate indicator and service sharing
screens.lead: Compare the hit rate by provider, cache lifetime, and shared scope as shown in the table. Also refer to the definition of hit rate provided below.

data.caption: Cache verification methods and lifespans, shared scope by provider
rows: The document advises to send similar prefix requests within a short period of time.
The minimum number of input tokens per model must be filled, and if matched, the reduction is automatically transmitted.
Prompt Caching Dashboard's cache read hit rate, diagnose tool to verify reasons for miss
Basic 30 minutes, the Responses API allows a minimum validity period of 12 hours.
You can group requests with `prompt_cache_key`; maintaining a session does not guarantee a cache hit.
Response `usage` for `cache_creation_input_tokens` and `cache_read_input_tokens`, organizational-wide trend analysis via Usage and Cost API
Basic 5 minutes, refreshed each time it is used, with a 1-hour lifespan being twice the basic input price.
Caching is isolated between organizations and is also isolated at the workspace level in the Claude API.
data.notes: Hit rate is the value obtained by dividing the number of input tokens processed via cache by the total number of input tokens, and it must be calculated separately per service to identify whether a particular service has structural issues. Service sharing is achieved by using a common prefix for standard guidelines and reference documents, with service-specific differences appended afterward. However, in cases like Anthropic where caching is partitioned by workspace, services residing in different workspaces will not share cache even if they use the same prefix. For cost optimization, guidelines recommend first measuring usage before implementing measures to reduce waste.

screens.outro: Having verified the criteria for measurement and sharing, let's apply them to the example.

screens.title: Explanation: When the success rate is low due to different system prompts for each service.
screens.lead: The instructor breaks down the example step by step. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

steps.title: Verify the example
steps.body: Customer support, sales, and HR services use the same company policy document but start their system prompts with different sentences. Caching is enabled, but cost savings are minimal.

steps.title: Measures hit rate by service
steps.body: The cache token field of responses is aggregated by service to calculate hit rates. All three services show low values. This is a step of verifying the problem with numbers, not speculation.

steps.title: Compare the beginning of the prompt
steps.body: We compare the prompt beginnings of the three services side by side. Since the service names and tone guidelines appear at the front, their prefixes differ from the outset. Although the same policy document follows afterward, the differing beginnings indicate that reusability has not occurred. This stage reveals that the root cause is not the model or the provider, but in the prompt structure itself.

steps.title: Common content will be collected ahead.
steps.body: Collect common policy documents and common rules at the front, and move service-specific guidelines to follow them. Now the prefixes of the three services are identical up to the end of the entire policy document.

steps.title: Caching is reused across services
steps.body: Since requests with the same prefix are issued in a short period of time, one service's cache can be accessed by another service. However, in places where caching is isolated at the workspace level, such as Anthropic, all three services must be invoked within the same workspace.

steps.title: Re-measure the hit rate
steps.body: After modifying the structure, measure the success rate per service again to verify improvements. If no improvement is observed, sequentially check the minimum token count, request interval, and variability within prefixes. Following this order allows quickly narrowing down the root cause.

screens.outro: Next, we'll examine a common trap involving prefix disruption.

screens.title: Explanation: A common fluctuating factor that disrupts the prefix
screens.lead: When you select an item to expand, a trap that breaks the prefix appears along with the recommended response from the instructor. Please read it, considering whether your service includes any of the listed items.

items.title: Trap 1: Current timestamp and request ID of the frontmost entry
items.body: This is the most common trap. Since the value changes with each request, the prefix does not match from the start. Move it to the back or include it only when the model absolutely needs to know it.

items.title: Trap 2: Tool list ordered differently per user
items.body: The tool definition includes a prefix, which changes each time the order is requested, even if the content remains the same. Fix the order of the tool list.

items.title: Trap 3: Concatenating documents in a different order for each request
items.body: When reference documents are attached in the order of search results, groups of the same document will each receive a different prefix every time. By defining a sorting rule, the same document will be attached in the same order.

items.title: Trap 4: Short prefix insufficient to meet minimum token count
items.body: If the prefix is shorter than the minimum length specific to the model, it will not be cached. Errors do not occur, making it hard to notice. Common content is moved further forward to pad the length.

items.title: Trap 5: Long request intervals causing cache expiration
items.body: Even if they share the same prefix, they are reprocessed once their lifespan expires. Since Anthropic includes response generation time within the lifespan, subsequent requests after a long response generation must consider timing. Adjust call frequency and lifespan accordingly.

items.title: Trap 6: Each service maintains its own separate documentation guidelines
items.body: If each service manages its own instruction documents, slight inconsistencies in wording and different prefixes can occur. Instead, common prefixes are managed in one place and shared across services.

screens.outro: Now I will summarize the previous content into a single reference point.

screens.title: Summary: Standardizing prefixes increases accuracy rate.
screens.lead: Summarizing the content discussed so far.

paragraphs: Caching stores processed states rather than tokens, and is reused only when the same prefix is found at the beginning of the prompt. The principle of structure is to place common content at the front and variable content at the back.

Hit rate is measured per service, while the common prefix is shared across services. The extent of sharing depends on the provider's cache isolation unit, so the call location must also be verified. Repeatedly measuring, restructuring, and remeasuring in this manner can significantly reduce cost and latency for shared contexts in large-scale services. Conversely, if the structure is not changed and only functionality is enabled, costs will persist without achieving any benefit.

glossary.def: A feature that reuses previously processed input states from requests sharing the same prefix, reducing cost and delay.
This is a design that maintains identical common content at the beginning of the prompt across the service and request sides.
The ratio of tokens processed via caching out of the total input tokens. It must be calculated separately by service to identify issues.
Multiple services use the same common prefix to leverage caches created by each other.

misconceptions.myth: Enabling caching always results in savings.
misconceptions.fact: If the prefixes vary each time, accuracy will not be achieved. Simply turning on is insufficient; the prompt structure must be designed.

misconceptions.myth: The response of the model is stored in the cache.
misconceptions.fact: According to the OpenAI documentation, what is stored is not the token or the response, but the input processing state. Newly arrived input still needs to be processed.

misconceptions.myth: A hit is guaranteed if only a session is maintained.
misconceptions.fact: OpenAI documentation explains that cache hits are not guaranteed even when a session is maintained. Hit rates must be verified as a metric.

closing.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.
points: General content comes first, variable content comes later.
Hit rate is measured per service.
The common prefix is shared among services but identifies the unit wherein caching is isolated.

closing.reflection: In the prompts of our services, how similar are the first 1,000 tokens across each other?

checks.q: Prompt caching is enabled, yet almost no savings are visible in the invoice. What is the most likely cause of the prompt structure?
options: Place common guidelines first, followed by the user's question.
Similar-prefixed requests are received in a short period of time.
At the front, the current time or user name is entered, and the prefix changes each request.
Always fix the order of the tool list to be the same.
checks.explain: Cache reuses only the invariant prefix that follows from the beginning of the prompt. If the initial value changes every time, matching will not occur even if the rest is identical.

wrong.0: This structure, which places common content first and variable content later, improves accuracy.
wrong.1: Repetition within a short time period is a condition for reuse within the cache lifetime.
wrong.3: Fixing the order ensures the prefix remains consistent, which is advantageous for alignment.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. Results are not recorded.

checks.q: Pair factors that disrupt prefixes with appropriate responses.
left: Current timestamp and request ID at the front
Tool list in different order per user
Documents concatenated in order specific to each request
Request intervals grow longer, causing cache expiration.
right: Specifies alignment rules to establish a consistent order.
Matches call frequency with cache lifetime
Move back or insert only when necessary
checks.explain: Prefixes are not reusable if they differ by just one character. Variable values should be pushed back, order should be fixed, and call intervals must be kept within the cache lifetime.
